Yes, I know I'm necroposting. Actually I'm necroposting on a response to a necropost of a necropost. But I have some things to say that may interest people today so I'm gonna say it. Real life MD/PhD neuroscientist here, specifically molecular biology of stress and the serotonin system. There is no dose of an SSRI (or SNRI), or non-selective SRI/NRI that will produce a large enough effect ot come close. They just don't attenuate severe acute stimulus driven fear enough. You might be able to do it with a benzodiazepine, but you'd probably be close to unconscious if not unconscious . You wouldn't remember much if anything that's for sure.

Three words: bilateral amygdala lesions.

+ Show
- Hide

Bilateral amygdala lesions decease (if partial) or eliminate )(if complete) the ability to experience fear. Complete bilateral congenital absence of the amygdala results in essentially compete absence of fear. Wired article was that too light? How about this:
One major exception CO2 inhalation will still produce panic even without amygdale, sometimes causing people to experience fear for the first time in their lives. (disclosure, I got my degrees where this work was done and have some professional connections with a couple of the authors)

On tryptophan and the othet aromatic amino acids

- Hide

Tryptophan is the ammo acid that serotonin and melatonin are made from, just as tyrosine is the amino acid that norepinephrine, dopamine, and epinephrine and melanin) are made from. Humans can synthesize tryrosine from phenylalanine but phenylalanine and tryptophan must be obtained fron the diet. The casein in (the inaptly named) non-diary creamer is high in all 3 of these amino acids.

item.content:encoded:
Don't confuse new studies with confirmed fact. That's how you get nonsense like "vaccines cause autism": one researcher decided they were going to overturn established theory, and played with the data until it gave them the answer they wanted.

It's also important to differentiate between things like clinical ophidophobia that makes someone freak out at a picture of a snake, and ophidophobia in the sense that made my laid-back cat (who has never seen a snake in his life) go full arched-back hiss at a coiled water hose that admittedly did sort of look like a snake. One is a pure fear, the other is more closely related to disgust.

"The source of this fear is not clear, but appears to be similar in nature to arachnophobia and ophidiophobia, originating on a pre-conscious, genetic level."

Although the idea that fears of spiders and snakes is somehow biological is commonly believed, and has been studied in the past, there are many more recent studies that support instead the idea that they are merely cultural. Although I understand that there is no true 'explanation' as to the origin of these fears, it pains me to see a purportedly scientific organization like the Foundation believing a common civilian misconception. Even if one doesn't accept that these fears are cultural, there's certainly not more reason to believe that they are biological, so the Foundation shouldn't be casually stating it as a scientific fact.

item.content:encoded:
Additionally, there is a SPECIFIC example of this phenomenon having been used by science - figuring out where to reintroduce a herbivorous chinese animal (I think some kind of deer but the memory is hazy) that had gone extinct in the wild but successfully bred up to a sustainable population through the various individuals kept in zoos and foreign reserves (and no small amount of IVF and frozen embryos).

+ show block
– hide block

Thing is, it went extinct from hunting so long ago that those who had collected live specimens didn't accurately record where they had been collected from, other than in a relatively large area, with great natural diversity and a lot of geographic barriers between sub zones… and they didn't want to cause yet another invasive-species problem, in the interest of correcting a human-caused extinction.

The trick to working out where to release them relied entirely on instinctive, genetic threat-response. They went out with tape recorders, captured the calls, roars, etc of as many extant predators in the area as possible, and carefully noted where each recording was made. Then they played the recordings to a bunch of the release candidate herbivores.

Most of the tapes elicited no particular response, or only an occasional reaction of slight concern or curiosity to some of the sounds, most often the alarm calls of birds (which can of course travel more easily and widely). Only a few, all from a certain fairly small area, produced the classical prey-animal fear response, and did so quite strongly. Repeating the test had the same result. The animal's natural geographical place in the food chain had been rediscovered - even though none of the living population had ever encountered that area's resident predators or their calls before, and vice versa. The release was organised to happen in that one region, and by all accounts they settled right in almost as if they'd never gone away, both in live, what they consumed, and what consumed them, and in what quantity…

(and one presumes there would have been additional tests using predator faeces from the different areas, cut-out photographs of their faces popped up on sticks over a wall, the unique plants to see which ones they found most strongly attractive or repulsive (with an indifference response being more of a black mark than either), etc…)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Genetic aversion to certain things - or in other words, instinctive fear - has totally been proven. And the evolutionary method behind it is blood simple; if there's some kind of primary existential threat, whether passive or active, that an organism needs to avoid at all cost in order to survive long enough to reproduce and raise its young to independence… then, apart from the lucky few that never encounter that threat or get to learn from others' mistakes, the only ones that pass on their genes are those that carry DNA mutations that code for an autonomous fear response to that threat.

+ show block
– hide block

Brains and their autonomic routines don't spring out of nowhere. Everything your body does autonomically has come about through that same system.

And often the response will be tuned to the specific threat. A particularly dangerous area or type of topography (volcano, high ground with a sheer drop, dark cave that could be hiding noturnal predators or sharp, slippery rocks)? Keep the fuck away from there, back away from edge, don't go in the hole…
A twitch or pursuit predator that can move faster and with more agility than you, but responds largely to movement rather than being good at picking out static detail, especially given the natural camouflage you may have against the environment or line-of-sight advantage where you may spy it whilst still hidden in cover? (pouncing snakes, scorpions, flying insects, medium size predatory vertebrates… also, zombies) Keep the fuck still. Stay quiet, breathe shallow. Don't take your eyes/ears off it. Wait it out, as it will almost certainly eventually disregard any small hint it might have received to your presence after a time and move on to seeking prey elsewhere, after which you can relax and book it on out of there.
Small venomous things or violent predators that you can more easily outpace? Run the fuck away. Maybe get a bit of distance then turn around and batter the shit out of it if you've got a reasonable chance of being able to kill it without seriously hurting or poisoning yourself, so you don't have to worry about it tracking you and reappearing later.
Poisonous foods? Your tastebuds will have evolved to make it taste foul. Spit it out.
Foods of limited nutritional value? They'll taste bland, and you'll feel compelled to find something with more energy and vitamins once immediate hunger is dealt with.
Rival of your own species challenging you for mating rights, or threatening your mate and young, or their being threatened by a predator you can probably fight off or at least distract long enough for them to escape? Or if your nest or tools or food reserves or shiny things you use to make yourself look more fuckable are at risk of destruction or theft? You'd better get good and angry, so you're in a fighting mood…

All that stuff. It's all hard coded. It's why it's so hard to fight, why people who aren't sufficiently self-aware of their own emotions and responses can act in extremely animalistic, irrational, exaggerated, and indeed "stupid" ways… even if they're otherwise not of particularly low intellect.

It's also why very few people go toppling obliviously off of high structures (even babies) unless they're disabled, drugged, or under some other altered state of mind, or make some indirect mistake (climbing and slipping, for example). It's also why you tend not to get vertigo unless you look towards the drop, even if your position in space and bodily orientation hasn't changed.

Generally it's protective and beneficial, except in the cases where mutation and natural selection hasn't yet quite caught up. Human monkey-like irrational, vindictive tribal behaviour in adult, political relations, even where it's entirely unwarranted is one example - what might have worked in the jungle, with stones and tree branches as weapons and sparse enough populations that big fights only happened very infrequently, is a massive liability in the modern world. Especially as we haven't quite gotten over the whole "choose the silverback as tribe leader" instinct yet. A lot of natural stress and withdrawal responses that would have actually been generally protective back in prehistory, or at least (in the case of depression) helped ease the pain of an individual that was in a hopeless position and on an otherwise slow and anguished path towards death (and would so withdraw from the group, stop eating, act in careless ways that might put them in danger of predation, hastening the end before things get too terrible - as pets can sometimes seen to do), are entirely at odds with a lot of the challenges we face in the modern world, which end up erroneously setting them off strongly and frequently, especially in those who might, a quarter million years ago, have actually been more likely to survive because of their enhanced emotional reactions.

And then there's this type of reaction, the motion-sensitive-predator one, which the skip is managing to trigger off… whether justiably, or entirely erroneously. In the containment site, it manifests as people being terrified to push through doors, even though the most likely outcome is that they bring more than 10% of the creature into view, causing it to vanish… to the point where they spend hours, or days, balled up in a state of entirely witless, immobile, shallow breathing terror, even to the point where they expire from dehydration or some other threat that provokes a less powerful motivational stimulus even though it's actually far more dangerous.
On a lonely secondary highway through a remote forested area, it manifests as deer or other such animals, wandering around in their normal way, being surprised by an approaching vehicle - especially at night - and registering it, with it general size, shape, and position of its glowing eyes (they have no way to know they're internally lit, rather than retroreflective of the moon) pushing all the "twitch predator" buttons as hard as possible. And what reaction does that provoke? STAY THE FUCK STILL. Even though they aren't at all camouflaged against the artificial blacktop, as they would have been against the natural forest. And the onrushing car or truck isn't actually an active threat to it, other than in terms of running it down if it doesn't step quickly out of the way.
(And also the other even stranger response of running in front of a passing vehicle when they would have been entirely safe if they'd stood still at the side… in that case, most likely the "distract pursuit predator that's coming terrifyingly close to mate/young by gaining its attention and hope to escape by getting enough of a head start before it can fully change course and start to catch up". With a side dish of not being prepared for the sheet speed of said predator, as it looks closer and slower than it actually is due to the size, and their lack of wide angle long-range depth perception, and doesn't exhibit the expected startle response of turning towards their projected path instead of ploughing straight on…)

In essence… maybe this SCP is the car, and the Foundation staff are the forest animals. Except now they've got guns, and the environment doesn't even give them easy ways of avoiding the actually fairly sparse traffic. It's just minding its own business and doesn't mean any harm at all… its just that it doesn't, from the human point of view, belong in this place, the same way as the deer doesn't recognise the car as belonging to the forest, and so confusion heaps on top of freakout, and the result is Bad Times.

The question is … what is it now doing in its makeshift workshop? Is it something to help prevent against crashing into petrified fawns? Or maybe just to protect itself and scoop up the roadkill? Possibly even a system that will just shoot them to make the impact less and render the unavoidable death more humane? Even a disguise to no longer look like the animal's absolute worst nightmare?

…or turning itself into a tank covered in spikes, that can be driven through the forest with murderous glee, collecting wildlife as it goes?

And in the strange circles through which the SCP turns, that essentially means either a reclassification to Keter, or keeping it as Euclid and simply understanding more about it, so it may be more easily contained, neutralised, or even helped (or, if you like, protected)… though of course they don't often bother with that one so much.

And of course it might even have valuable knowledge about things other than itself to impart.

Or at least knowing more may help those faced with it remain calmer and more rational, and deal with the appearances in an aversion-therapy, CBT kind of way. And the foundation will get to find out what happens when you open the door.

item.content:encoded:
Simpler solution: Use an old school TV / video camera. One that uses a panopticon tube or similar. IE, essentially an inverse CRT, where a scanning beam picks up the image…

+ show block
– hide block

Though in fact, as that requires fairly bright light focussed onto a phosphor layer at the end (with the intensity detection using the beam in a similar way to a CRT memory storage tube), that may still count as creating a complete image. Instead, something more like a fully digital version of the original Baird TV setup may be better… not the one finally made use of in studios, but the actual original, which formed its output signal using an actual raster-scanning beam of light (which is what the Nipkow disc was for, as for some reason no-one thought to use a mirror on a gimbal and a couple of cams…) and a single non-imaging photocell.

So we take e.g. a Laser-LED projector (which uses the gimbal-mirror idea, much like an old skool vector-art laser beamer, but with slightly defocussed red and green lasers and a tightly focussed blue LED, to produce its images), set up a big ol' fresnel lens in front of it set to shrink rather than expand the image falling on it, with a focal distance adjusted *just-so* for the scans to all converge (horizontally, at least) right where they need to pass through the door, preferably fairly close with a very wide spread… and a single panchromatic light sensor positioned and lensed similarly to detect how much of the beam is absorbed and how much reflected (at least, diffusely).

Mod the projector somewhat to turn down the beam power and the scan speed so there's no way to argue even that persistence of vision with the ambient lights dimmed way down could count as a single coherent image - in fact, not even 10% of it, so its scanning appears extremely flickery and "rolling" to human eyes, and unsuitable for viewing normal material at all, and supply an input image sequence that is pure red, pure green, pure blue and timed to change during each effective Vsync period (similar to the effect sometimes experienced with a failing colour wheel motor in white light source/sequential-colour DLP units, but with the added fun of extreme desynchronisation to the point that the vertical scan is very noticeable and sensitive individuals might even detect some suggestion of horizontal scanning). Connect the photocell to something simple and non-imaging like a voice recorder (PCM, not MP3! Or preferably entirely analogue), with no added sync pulses or anything that may suggest it's being used to store visual rather than audio or computer data.

Set up facing the door of a lab and have everyone hang out in there for as long as it takes. Maybe do a little construction work beforehand so that there's sufficient food and water supply and also bathroom facilities - accessible without doors, but instead around simple labyrinthine privacy shields and access controlled by a *human* "doorman", on rotation.
(this may also help with an investigation into whether it's JUST doors, or anything that works to effectively conceal line-of sight for an otherwise straight path, should it then manifest within the privacy chicane… there may instead be a need for a simple low-rise curtain over which you could see at all times, but only by standing close enough… so again, everyone mutually agrees to behave)

When you hear heavy breathing and feel a weird sense of dread, turn on the recorder (and, heck, you could probably get away with an extremely simple edison phonograph type system should there be a sufficiently straightforward way for light to turn into sound… very hard to interfere with, though the breathing would also be recorded), and fire up the projector… Thankfully, Laser-LED models have near-zero warm up time, and the main delay is the control board going through POST, which itself can be shortened by setting standby mode to "ready" rather than "eco"; a device to supply suitable signals to the video input ports could be made from extremely basic parts (a 3-bit cascade counter or looping shift register that cycles around, putting 0.75v one of the RGB lines and 0v on the other two, with the shift triggered by the transition of "bright light" to "no light" measured by a sensor picking up the more diffuse radiation off the beam, or maybe just sat at one extreme corner of the output area with a few milliseconds of refractory period, plus a simple two-part sync generator - standard VGA would be more than ample) and left running at all times.

Take the output from that, feed it into some remote computer, create a WAV file at as high a notional frequency as you can manage (as creating a coherent picture on a standard-def TV requires at least a couple MHz of bandwidth, and we won't have slowed it down *that* much - of course, if we want to do this at 192 or even 384khz, we'll need specialist recording kit in the first place, though it helps that our primary sensor is a photocell and not an ultrasound microphone, so a tape recorder rigged to spool the tape through at much higher speed than normal (about as fast as full FFWD/RWD in a good deck), using very high quality tape and an extended-response head and circuitry (all filters removed) will be needed… thankfully, we don't need more than a few seconds of recording time, so even a fairly low capacity cassette will be more than ample… and in fact it'll be entirely acceptable to play it back at normal speed into a fairly ordinary PC at a normal sampling rate because it doesn't matter much if it's a long, slowed down signal sampled at a low rate, or a short, full speed one sampled at extra high rate), cut the portion of interest into three pieces, trim each one to start and end exactly in sync with the first and last scanlines, or as best they can be estimated… Save to .RAW data files… load each into an image editor as a greyscale picture (at which point it should already be possible to resolve some kind of obvious detail - getting the dimensions right during the import shouldn't be too hard as we know how many lines were scanned, from the projector's native resolution, and the pixels per line just have to be twiddled so that it produces a reasonably straight-sided pic with a darker bar down the right hand side and what is effectively missing data right at the end of the bottom line, with no horizontal duplication or obvious interlacing effects), and composite a full colour image using the three separate channels. Possibly it may be useful to leave various artefacts of known (particularly primary or pure secondary, plus high contrast black-white) colouration within the range of the beam and photocell so to make registration easy at this stage as it's indeterminate which colour will scan first and we don't want to guess at it TOO much…

Voila, a simple method with a very complicated explanation…

Or in other words… modify a laser-LED projector to slow-scan one primary colour at a time, through a lens that allows something akin to limited tomography through the gap between the doors, connected to a photocell and high speed (analogue?) data recorder. Take that data, and use a remote PC to reconstruct the non-image data into first three monochrome separations, and then a full colour composite.
(after which you may need to do quite a bit of perspective-correction…)

At no point is more than a tiny fraction of the creature "visible" to the sensors, even through overshine or any kind of persistence, and in any case they're entirely non-imaging in themselves (and in fact might suffer a bit of blur from the diffuse reflection effects, like a more limited form of fogging).

Of course, your big problem is that seeing the ENTIRE creature could constitute some kind of extreme memetic cognitohazard (given that fractions considerably less than one-tenth, or even just a tiny glimpse plus the breathing sound, causes people to mentally BSOD through terror), even at the B&W separation stage, and anyone attempting to process or reconstruct the picture will invariably end up shitting themselves so bad that they die within seconds. Or to be more professional about it, it'll cause such an extreme fear reaction that the subject will simultaneously experience a catastrophic seizure, a neurotransmitter storm on the sympathetic system which causes all innervated organs to either shut down so hard they effectively die OR go into overdrive and quickly overheat / rupture / otherwise fatally damage themselves, and their limbic/endocrine system produces a hard spike of adrenaline into the bloodstream to the effect that the adrenal and other source glands shrivel up and haemorrhage, and any organ not already fucked by nervous psychosomatic overload will be shocked over the line when that slug of stimulant (or alternatively, from their perspective, depressant) hits. Assuming of course the heart is still beating in a coherent fashion by then (instead of either going into fibrilliation or plain flatlining), hasn't ruptured anywhere, and the arterial system is still sufficiently intact. All ultimately topped off with a multi-site overpressure-induced stroke of epic proportions coincident with several other vital organs suffering severe physical damage from the sudden massive increase in systolic pressure.

Or in other words they will quite literally die of fright, or from a technical medical perspective, acute clinical shock. In a way that will make any first responders on the scene wonder if they're witnessing some new rapid-onset form of ebola. Before glancing at the computer screen and also being immediately brainfucked by this unexpected new basilisk…

tl;dr be careful what you wish for. 1920s earth science was more than sufficient for the purposes of getting some kind of full body image of this skip, but… *do you REALLY want to*?!

(Edit: an additional way to avoid the "imaging" thing being suggested a plain scanning beam, and there's enough time in a typical incident to get away with it, we can use a more complicated signal generator… one that feeds similarly monochromatic primary coloured data into the projector, but much more sparsely, with the frame actually being mostly dark with randomly placed bright dots - perhaps, just to be sure, at a ratio of 1:11? - and said speckled patterns generated with an algorithm that keeps track of which pixels have already been lit up in previous frames, so that between the 33 patterns pulsed out of the projector, the entirely of the detectable scene on the other side of the door is cumulatively illuminated, maybe over the course of 3 or 4 seconds overall. This also means that if it dematerialises partway into the process, a lower resolution approximation of its appearance can be reconstructed with a bayer-like interpolation filter (an alternative approach, if it turns out the "10%" is more in terms of outline than sheer total area, could be to have even sparser individual squares, or low density stripes contained within a small fraction of the overall scan, per image, so there's much less chance of either an outline or an overall amount of it adding up to 10% being lit at once; this may require running the projector at its normal scan rate instead, and using input images that are sequentially identical in each colour field, with a fourth period that's completely black, in order to avoid any kind of persistence with large parts of the creature appearing sort of visible for a split second, just with different 1-bit primary/secondary colours patterned across it like a quilt…).
It also means the risk of a worker reconstructing the picture ending up seeing something that's sufficiently clear in any one frame to cause the death-from-scary effect is much reduced.
Registration would be difficult of course, especially without introducing something that might seem like an obvious, regular sync pulse. Maybe guarantee a certain small number of dots in each that are along the first/last line and appear at the extreme start/end of a line, especially in the corners, but not in the same place horizontally on the terminal lines or on the same line at the limits of horizontal scan with each frame - in that way the edges are reasonably obvious (especially with the surrounding completely dark sync areas) and a firm alignment should be possible, even with the middle half of the picture area software-obscured for intellectual safety.

Or, it could even be automated using software that has the original pattern produced by the random image generator available for comparison purposes and can use probability curve matching and other such statistical voodoo to identify each one, which would be particularly useful in the limited-area cases where the projected light would be a series of unique, non-symmetric (reflective or rotational) barcode-like patterns in each sub-area, not so easy for a human to deal with but easy for a computer to extract and reconstruct in order to determine where the actual outline should be even if there's no obvious discontinuity AT the edge.

Once properly aligned, as best as possible, the layers are flattened together using an additive (rather than averaging) filter for each separate channel - any speckling or colour abberations caused by suboptimal alignment left as-is because of the sheer difficulty of being able to judge whether or not it actually DOES look like that in reality, and the fairly minor impact on overall quality - then composited into colour and perspective corrected in the normal way.

And given to some poor bastard who really pissed off the Overseers to test whether the fear effect is still transmitted through still 2D pictures. Though to be kind, they will at least allow the test subject to be doped up to the eyes with anxiolytics (both SSRI, SNRI, and others), paralytics and adrenaline receptor blockers, with a touch of heroin on top just to add a final touch of mellow, with just enough consciousness and coherency to actually look at and describe what they're looking at… first time round. I mean, still gotta find out if it actually DOES scare people to death normally, after seeing whether it's safe to look at under extreme sedation.)

Ok, this article feels like it was written to terrify me specifically. I used to very frequently (still sometimes) have hallucinations/delusions involving something that looks almost exactly the same as 303. Here's one such method using no mechanical or electronic parts, only a single lens and a long tube.

At least, no mechanical or electronic parts anywhere near the skip, which may turn out to be an important distinction.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I propose we monitor the 2nd floor storage room until such time as it is no longer inhabited, then quickly send maintenance in to drill a hole in the wall. Cap the end of the hole with a fisheye lens and insert a metal tube with a mirrored interior, and you've got the basis of a pinhole camera you can operate from the other end of the tube.

We can extend that tube to a few feet, or a few hundred feet, all without introducing any mechanical or electronic parts.

At the far end of the tube, we focus the light coming down the tube to resolve our actual image. This is captured via charge-coupled device (CCD) sensors, such as those used in a slightly older model digital camera. However, unlike a digital camera, these will be programmed to activate and deactivate in a sequence, rather than all at once. Since each sensor will "read" only a single pixel, much less than 10% of the entity is resolved at any one time. When the data is composited into an image later, which could be done offsite, in a highly-visible open space surrounded by long-range telescopic cameras. It could even be compiled at multiple locations simultaneously, or compiled "on the cloud" and streamed live to multiple terminals in various locations as it resolves.

In short, while we may not understand SCP-303's method of movement, we know enough to take a picture of it in such a way that preventing us from developing the picture causes more even pictures to be taken.
